worst_places.after:
With a regular (non-private) property, `other.balance` just returns `undefined` when the property is missing. Property access is permissive by design: "not here" is a normal answer, not an error.

Private fields are deliberately stricter. `#secret` is tied to the brand of one specific class definition. Reading it on an object that class never constructed is a genuine type error, not a missing value.

The engine knows the difference between the two cases. "This object has no such private field because it is not an instance of that class" is a real mistake — for example, passing the wrong kind of object to a method that expects one class's instance. So the engine throws instead of returning `undefined`, because a silent `undefined` would hide that bug.

worst_places.after:
**Why Temporal is immutable:** the bug above comes from two things together — `Date` is mutable, and objects are passed by reference. One piece of code changes the shared `Date`, and every other piece of code holding that same object sees the change.

Temporal removes this whole group of bugs: every operation returns a *new* object instead of changing the existing one. It is the same rule people already follow for state updates in modern apps, and the same reason you avoid mutating arrays and objects directly elsewhere in JS.

worst_places.before:
**The default sort behavior — and why it breaks for numbers:**
```javascript
const numbers = [10, 1, 21, 2];
console.log(numbers.sort()); // [1, 10, 2, 21] — NOT sorted numerically!
```
Without a comparator function, `sort()` converts each element to a **string** and compares them lexicographically
worst_places.after:
By default `sort()` converts every element to a string and sorts those strings alphabetically — so numbers come out in the wrong order. It also sorts the array in place, changing the original.

```javascript
const numbers = [10, 1, 21, 2];
console.log(numbers.sort()); // [1, 10, 2, 21] — NOT sorted numerically!
```
Compared character by character, like in a dictionary, `'10'` sorts before `'2'` because `'1'` comes before `'2'`. The actual numeric value is ignored completely.

worst_places.quote: Common pitfall: implementing an async iterator's `.next()` as a regular (non-`async`) function that manually constructs and returns a Promise wrapping `{ value, done }` — this works correctly (an `async function` automatically wraps its return value in a Promise, but a plain function returning a Promise explicitly achieves the same contract), but it's an easy place to accidentally forget the Promise wrapper entirely and return the plain object directly, which silently breaks `for await...of`'s expectation that every `.next()` call yields something awaitable.

worst_places.before: Common pitfall: implementing an async iterator's `.next()` as a regular (non-`async`) function that manually constructs and returns a Promise wrapping `{ value, done }` — this works correctly (an `async function` automatically wraps its return value in a Promise, but a plain function returning a Promise explicitly achieves the same contract), but it's an easy place to accidentally forget the Promise wrapper entirely and return the plain object directly, which silently breaks `for await...of`'s expectation that every `.next()` call yields something awaitable.
worst_places.after: Common pitfall: writing `.next()` as a plain (non-`async`) function that builds and returns the Promise by hand. This is correct in itself — an `async function` wraps its return value in a Promise automatically, and a plain function returning a Promise explicitly meets the same contract. The risk is forgetting the wrapper and returning the plain `{ value, done }` object instead. `for await...of` expects every `.next()` call to return something awaitable, so it breaks silently.

patterns: The 'Common pitfall / Частая ловушка' closer is a fixed structural habit and a fixed defect: 128 of 129 answers end with one, 113 of those are a single sentence, and in EN 117 of 126 exceed the sentence limit (average 58 words, worst 111; RU average 34, worst 78). Because it is the last thing on screen it is the most-remembered slot in every answer, and it is reliably the hardest sentence in the answer. Fix pattern: state the mistake in one short sentence, then the consequence in a second, then the correct alternative in a third — the technical content already decomposes into exactly those three.

Answers are built as 'label → code → explanation', and 11-12 of 129 never write the answer as prose at all: q-44, q-62, q-89, q-90 open with a raw code fence, and q-1, q-13, q-28, q-34, q-54 (en), q-71, q-100 open with a bolded section label that restates the question. A further group leads with the wrong thing on purpose: q-92 opens with the pre-ES2022 WeakMap workaround, q-98 with the recursive version that the question asks to replace, q-100 and q-114 with the problem rather than the answer. Rubric C would go from 3-4 to 5 by prepending one plain-words sentence — no other change needed.

RU and EN are not the same text at two lengths — they are two different drafts. For q-1..q-109 the EN prose is 1.8× the RU (up to 3.9× at q-109), and the difference is almost entirely the consolidating paragraph that follows a code block and explains what just happened; RU deletes it. For q-110..q-129 the ratio is 1.05, i.e. a faithful translation. The result is that EN and RU fail different rubrics: EN carries the explanation but in 60-135-word sentences (B/F), while RU is crisp but has had the explanation removed (D) — including, at q-56, the one sentence that actually answers the question asked. Any fix pass has to decide 'restore into RU, then shorten in both', not treat one locale as the source of truth.

RU quality splits sharply by difficulty tier. The junior/middle answers are clean, living Russian; the senior/advanced tier accumulates a layer of transliterated jargon that has no gloss and cannot be looked up — 'резолвится' (12×), 'вычищает очередь' as a calque of 'drain the queue' (16×), 'settle-ится' (7×), 'коэрсит' (6×), 'крашит/крашнуть' (7×), 'yield-нуть', plus calques like 'чиста для написания' and 'не подлежащий сборке мусора namespace'. Notably the classic bureaucratic markers are absent (2× «является», zero «осуществляется»/«данный»), so this is a jargon problem, not a register problem.
notes: Three code examples are genuinely broken in both locales, not just hard to read: an unescaped \n in the JSON turned into a real newline at q-17 (the multi-line-string example now shows an unterminated single-quoted string spanning three lines, demonstrating the opposite of its point), q-124 (`.join('` split across lines) and q-127 (`// "a` split across lines). Worth fixing before any language pass. Separately, q-81 explains stale closures using useState/useEffect without saying it is React or what a dependency array is — the only place in the bank where an answer depends on a framework the reader may not know. 293 EN / 272 RU code lines exceed 92 characters, nearly all because of right-aligned trailing comments that will wrap on a phone anyway.
